metadata.title: feat(mailfn): add reusable programmable mailbox function

items.body:
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Claim parse jobs before writing derived records**

When two at-least-once Queue deliveries for the same message execute concurrently, both can read `pending` here and pass this guard before either saves `ready`. Each invocation then generates different attachment IDs and writes attachments, usage records, threads, and parsed events, leaving duplicate attachments and accounting records plus potentially orphaned threads. Atomically claim the message for parsing, or make every derived write deterministic and idempotent.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve retryability when releasing storage reservations**

If cancellation encounters a transient D1 failure while releasing the durable storage reservation, this code has already consumed the only in-memory preflight token and then suppresses the error. A subsequent cancellation is therefore a no-op, and no scheduled reconciliation removes the orphaned `mailfn_storage_reservations` row, so its bytes count against the project forever and repeated failures can permanently exhaust inbound storage quota.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Keep provider-derived authentication evidence authoritative**

When an ingress adapter supplies trusted `authenticationResults` but the raw MIME also contains an `Authentication-Results` header, the parser-derived value wins here. Because that parsed value does not validate the trusted authentication service and can differ from the provider evidence, consumers may see forged or stale SPF/DKIM/DMARC results as the message's authoritative sender identity; retain the ingress result or explicitly distinguish trusted and untrusted parsed headers.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Claim migration versions atomically**

On a fresh deployment that relies on the factory's default runtime migration, two concurrent Worker events can both observe that version 1 is absent, run the idempotent DDL, and then race to insert the same migration-version primary key. The losing handler fails even though the schema is ready, which can reject an initial HTTP or email event; use a transaction or conflict-safe version claim instead of a separate check followed by a plain insert.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Mark fixtures disposed only after cleanup succeeds**

If `deleteInbox` fails transiently, `disposed` has already been set, so a retry from user cleanup or another lifecycle hook silently returns without deleting the inbox. This defeats retry-safe cleanup and leaves test inboxes and their stored evidence behind; set the flag only after successful deletion, or reset it when deletion rejects.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Validate inbox status before persisting it**

When the PATCH API receives an out-of-type JSON value such as `{ "status": "deleted" }`, `updateInbox` persists it without runtime validation. An inbox-scoped credential has `inbox:write` but not `inbox:delete`, so it can use this to make the inbox unreachable while bypassing `deleteInbox`'s retention-lock check, object cleanup, credential revocation, and deletion audit; restrict the accepted values to `active` and `disabled` before saving.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Avoid resurrecting a concurrently revoked credential**

If `revokeCredential` runs after `authenticate` reads an active credential but before this save, the stale object written here restores `status: 'active'` over the revoked row. A request already in flight can therefore undo revocation and leave the credential usable indefinitely; update only `lastUsedAt` conditionally while the durable status is still active rather than replacing the whole record.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve BCC recipients on idempotent SES sends**

When `idempotencyKey` is supplied—which MailFn does for every draft—this condition forces the raw-email path. That composer emits `To` and `Cc` headers but no `Bcc` header, and its `SendRawEmailCommand` supplies no explicit `Destinations`, so every address in `params.bcc` is silently omitted from delivery; pass the envelope destinations to SES or otherwise preserve BCC in the raw path.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Honor Reply-To when creating reply drafts**

For inbound messages that specify a `Reply-To` address, `createReplyDraft` always targets the SMTP envelope sender instead. This sends replies to bounce handlers or other transport addresses rather than the sender-designated mailbox; initialize recipients from `message.replyTo` when present and fall back to `envelopeFrom` only when it is absent.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject failed SendFn transactions instead of queuing them**

When a provider attempt fails, the checked-in SendFn persists a `failed` transaction and throws; on a retry with the same draft idempotency key, it returns that transaction from `EmailService.sendEmail`. This mapping treats `failed` like `pending`, reports the draft as `sending`, retains the outbound quota reservation, and prevents subsequent retries from reaching the provider. Handle failed transaction statuses as errors rather than converting every non-sent result to `queued`.

SFN-17 Build MailFn as a reusable programmable mailbox function

## Executive summary Capture the initial product and architecture direction for MailFn: a standalone, reusable Superfunctions capability for programmable mailboxes and inbound email workflows across Router and other projects. MailFn should begin as a focused, self-deployable mailbox runtime and preserve a clear boundary with SendFn. MailFn owns stateful inbox identities, inbound messages, retrieval, testing primitives, and mailbox lifecycle. SendFn remains responsible for outbound delivery and notification orchestration. ## Problem or opportunity Projects that automate acquisition, authentication, QA, and agent workflows need controlled email identities that can receive verification codes, magic links, lifecycle messages, and attachments through an API. Implementing this independently in each project would duplicate infrastructure, security controls, storage, and agent integrations. Superfunctions already provides shared foundations and an outbound communications function, making a reusable MailFn domain a natural extension. ## Expected outcome A validated MailFn product boundary and phased delivery plan that supports: * reusable deployment outside Router; * stable and expiring inbox identities; * Cloudflare-based inbound email processing; * agent-safe message retrieval and waiting; * a provider-neutral core with platform adapters; * composition with SendFn for outbound send and reply behavior; * a credible path from test inboxes to durable mailbox functionality. ## Goals * Define MailFn as an independently publishable Superfunctions domain. * Establish clear MailFn, SendFn, TestFn, and shared-package boundaries. * Design a minimal inbound-first release suitable for verification and lifecycle workflows. * Support SDK, CLI, and MCP access with scoped credentials. * Preserve raw evidence while applying explicit retention and secret-handling controls. * Keep the architecture reusable across multiple products and projects. ## Non-goals * Implement MailFn as part of this backlog-capture task. * Replace SendFn's outbound delivery responsibilities. * Launch a public arbitrary-recipient outbound email service in the initial release. * Commit to dates, staffing, pricing, or production availability. * Build a complete webmail client in the initial release. ## Acceptance criteria - ☐ The MailFn ownership boundary relative to SendFn and TestFn is documented and approved. - ☐ A provider-neutral core contract is defined for inboxes, messages, attachments, threads, scoped credentials, storage, and inbound transports. - ☐ A Cloudflare deployment design covers Email Routing, Workers, D1, R2, Queues, DNS, and failure handling. - ☐ The initial API covers stable and expiring inboxes, list/read/wait operations, filtering, OTP and verification-link extraction, retention, and revocation. - ☐ TypeScript SDK, CLI, and MCP surfaces are specified with least-privilege defaults. - ☐ Security covers OTP secrecy, credential scoping, webhook verification, idempotency, unknown-recipient rejection, retention, deletion, rate limits, and auditability. - ☐ Send/reply functionality is composed through SendFn rather than duplicated. - ☐ Testing covers MIME parsing, concurrent verification messages, attachments, retries, expiry, authorization boundaries, and Cloudflare failure modes. - ☐ A phased roadmap distinguishes the initial internal capability from later durable mailbox and public-platform functionality. - ☐ Release integration covers explicit workspace registration, package publication metadata, scoped CI, and a dedicated release gate. ## Dependencies and risks * Cloudflare Email Routing and Worker runtime behavior. * D1, R2, and Queue storage and delivery semantics. * Existing SendFn and shared delivery contracts on the Superfunctions next branch. * Explicit Superfunctions workspace and release-target registration. * Sensitive authentication content requires strict logging and retention controls. * Public outbound capability would introduce substantial abuse, reputation, suppression, and compliance responsibilities. * Default or newly created domains may be rejected by some products. * Existing Superfunctions worktrees contain unrelated changes; implementation should use a dedicated worktree. ## Open questions * Should the initial package family use `@mailfn/core` plus adapters, an unscoped `mailfn` facade, or both? * Should the first release be internal-only or generally publishable? * What are the default message and attachment retention periods? * Which APIs belong in MailFn versus an optional testing package? * Should OTP and verification-link extraction occur in the service, SDK, or MCP layer? * What tenancy boundary should separate projects and environments? * Which outbound operations, if any, are required for the first release? * What security and operational gates must be satisfied before custom-domain or public use? ## Supporting documents * [Ideation & Product Rationale — SFN-17: Build MailFn as a reusable programmable mailbox function]() * [Architecture & Delivery Plan — SFN-17: Build MailFn as a reusable programmable mailbox function]()
